prompt: A learner says that because light slows down when it enters water, it must lose energy, "which is why things look dimmer underwater". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong. Light does slow down, and that costs it no energy at all.
explanation: The speed of light in a medium is v = c ÷ n, so in water (n = 1.33) it travels at about 2.26 × 10⁸ m·s⁻¹ — the learner's premise is correct. But the energy of light is set by its FREQUENCY, E = hf, and the frequency does not change at a boundary: the wave on the far side is driven by the wave on the near side, cycle for cycle. What changes with the speed is the wavelength, λ = v ÷ f, which is why refraction bends the ray. The dimming underwater is real and has three other causes: some light is reflected at the surface instead of entering, water absorbs light as it travels (red first, which is why deep water looks blue), and scattering off suspended particles removes more. All three remove light from the beam; none of them makes a surviving photon weaker.

prompt: A jeweller explains that a diamond sparkles because "diamond is the hardest substance there is, so it takes the best polish". Evaluate the jeweller's reasoning.
answer: Hardness helps the finish but is not the cause. The sparkle comes from diamond's very high refractive index and the small critical angle that follows from it.
explanation: Diamond's refractive index is about 2.42, the highest of any common transparent material. From sin θc = 1 ÷ n, its critical angle is only about 24.4°, against roughly 41.8° for glass. Any ray meeting a facet at more than 24.4° from the normal is totally internally reflected, and because that angle is so small, almost every ray entering the stone bounces repeatedly inside rather than passing straight out — which is what a cutter's facet angles are chosen to exploit. The light eventually leaves through the top, concentrated, and diamond's strong dispersion splits it into colours on the way. The jeweller's fact is true and relevant in a minor way, since a hard material holds a sharper facet edge; a hard but low-index material would still not sparkle, and cubic zirconia, far softer, sparkles because its index is 2.15.

prompt: A learner claims that total internal reflection can be made to happen at any boundary "as long as you make the angle of incidence big enough". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong. It happens only when light travels from the optically denser medium toward the less dense one, no matter how large the angle.
explanation: Snell's law gives n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂. Going from a denser to a less dense medium (n₁ > n₂), the refracted ray bends AWAY from the normal, so θ₂ reaches 90° while θ₁ is still less than 90°; that value of θ₁ is the critical angle, and beyond it there is no refracted ray and all the light reflects. Going the other way (n₁ < n₂), the refracted ray bends TOWARD the normal, so θ₂ is always smaller than θ₁ and can never reach 90°. Even at an angle of incidence approaching 90°, light entering water from air still refracts, at about 48.8°. There is no critical angle in that direction at all, so increasing the angle cannot produce one. It is the pair of media and the direction of travel that decide whether total internal reflection is available; the angle only decides whether it happens.

prompt: A technician replaces the reflecting prisms inside a pair of binoculars with small silvered mirrors, reasoning that "a mirror is made for reflecting, so it must reflect better than a lump of glass". Evaluate the technician's reasoning.
answer: The reasoning is wrong. Total internal reflection in the prism returns essentially 100% of the light; a silvered mirror does not.
explanation: A metal coating absorbs some of every reflection — a good aluminium mirror returns about 90%, and binoculars use several reflections in sequence, so the losses compound. Total internal reflection has no absorbing layer at all: beyond the critical angle there is simply no refracted ray for the light to escape into, and effectively all of it reflects, every time. A glass prism also holds its two reflecting faces at a fixed 90° by the shape of the solid, whereas two separately mounted mirrors must be aligned and can drift. If the mirrors are silvered on the back, as ordinary household mirrors are, light must cross the glass twice and produces a faint second image from the front surface. The technician's instinct — that a purpose-built component beats an incidental one — is reasonable, and here the geometry of the glass is the purpose-built part.

prompt: A learner examining an endoscope claims it can only produce a clear image if the fibre bundle is kept straight, "because light travels in straight lines and will escape at any bend". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong. Light does travel in straight lines inside the fibre, and the bends are what keep it in.
explanation: Light in an optical fibre does travel in straight lines — between reflections. Each time it reaches the boundary between the core and the lower-index cladding it strikes at more than the critical angle, is totally internally reflected, and sets off in a new straight line. A gentle bend simply changes the angle at which the next reflection happens, and provided it stays above the critical angle the light stays trapped, which is why an endoscope can be threaded along a curved passage at all. The learner's premise is right and their conclusion would only follow for a SHARP bend: below a certain radius the angle of incidence drops under the critical angle and light does leak out, which is exactly why fibre has a stated minimum bend radius. What preserves the image is separate again — each fibre carries one picture element, and the fibres are held in the same relative positions at both ends.

prompt: A learner notes that a ray travelling along the normal passes into a glass block without bending, and concludes that it therefore does not slow down. Evaluate this conclusion.
answer: The conclusion is wrong. The ray slows exactly as much as any other; it simply has no direction to change.
explanation: The speed inside the glass is v = c ÷ n and depends only on the medium, not on the angle of arrival, so a ray entering along the normal slows to about 2 × 10⁸ m·s⁻¹ in glass of n = 1.5 like every other ray. Bending happens because one side of a wavefront enters the slower medium before the other and is held back, so the front pivots. A wavefront arriving along the normal meets the surface everywhere at once, so both sides slow together and there is nothing to pivot about — Snell's law says the same thing, since sin 0° = 0 makes θ₂ = 0 whatever n₂ is. The ray does change in a measurable way: its wavelength shortens in proportion, λ = v ÷ f, because the frequency is unchanged. The learner has treated bending as the evidence for slowing, when it is only the evidence for slowing UNEVENLY across the wavefront.

prompt: A cable supplier recommends the thickest available optical fibre for a long data link, on the grounds that "a wider core lets in more light, so the signal will be stronger and clearer". Evaluate the supplier's recommendation.
answer: Stronger, probably. Clearer, no — a wide core is the cause of the blurring that limits a long link.
explanation: A wider core does accept light over a larger range of angles, so more of it enters. That is also the problem. Rays entering at different angles travel by different numbers of reflections and therefore along paths of different lengths: a ray going almost straight down the axis arrives before one zig-zagging steeply, even though both travel at the same speed. A pulse sent in as a sharp spike emerges spread out, and on a long link consecutive pulses overlap until the receiver can no longer tell them apart. This is modal dispersion, and it is why long-distance links use SINGLE-MODE fibre with a core only about 9 µm across — narrow enough that essentially one path exists. The supplier has correctly identified how to collect more light and has chosen the design that destroys the timing, and on a data link it is the timing that carries the information.

prompt: A swimmer floating in a still pool notices that the surface looks like a mirror everywhere except a bright circular window directly overhead, and concludes that the pool lights must be faulty. Evaluate the swimmer's conclusion.
answer: The conclusion is wrong. This is what an underwater observer should see, and it follows from the critical angle of water.
explanation: Light reaching the swimmer's eye from the world above must cross the surface from air into water, and Snell's law compresses the entire 180° of sky into a cone. Rays arriving from the horizon refract to the largest possible angle inside the water, which is the critical angle, sin θc = 1 ÷ 1.33, giving θc ≈ 48.8°. So the whole of the sky, the trees and anyone standing at the edge appear squeezed into a circular window about 97° wide directly overhead — Snell's window. Outside that cone no light from above can arrive, and the swimmer instead sees the pool floor and walls reflected by total internal reflection at the underside of the surface, which is why it looks silvered. Nothing is faulty; a swimmer who saw the sky right out to the edges would be the observation needing explaining.

prompt: A learner states that total internal reflection occurs when light passes from a less dense medium into a denser one at a large angle, and offers light entering a glass block from air as an example. Evaluate the learner's claim.
answer: The claim has the direction reversed. The example is one in which total internal reflection can never occur.
explanation: Snell's law, n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂, decides this. Going from air into glass, n₂ is larger, so sin θ₂ is smaller than sin θ₁ and the refracted ray bends TOWARD the normal. Even at grazing incidence, θ₁ → 90°, the refracted ray only reaches about 41.8° in glass of n = 1.5, so a refracted ray always exists and light always gets in. Total internal reflection requires the opposite arrangement: from glass into air the ray bends AWAY from the normal, so θ₂ reaches 90° while θ₁ is still only 41.8°, and past that critical angle there is no direction left for a refracted ray to take, so all of the light reflects back into the glass. The learner's instinct that a large angle matters is right, and the condition on the angle only applies once the light is already in the denser medium and heading out.

prompt: A learner explains that bulbs in a series circuit glow less brightly the further they are from the battery, "because the current is used up as it goes round". Evaluate this explanation.
answer: The explanation is wrong on both counts: the bulbs are equally bright, and current is not consumed.
explanation: Charge is conserved and has nowhere to go in a single loop, so the current is identical at every point — an ammeter placed anywhere in the loop reads the same value, which is the measurement that settles it. Identical bulbs carrying identical current dissipate identical power, P = I²R, so they glow equally brightly whatever their order. What IS used up is ENERGY, not charge: each bulb converts some of the energy carried by the charge into light and heat, which shows as a potential difference across that bulb, and the sum of those potential differences equals the emf. The learner has confused the thing that flows with the thing that is delivered — like assuming water must disappear as it turns each of several water wheels in one channel.

prompt: A learner argues that household appliances are wired in parallel "so that each appliance receives the full current from the supply". Evaluate this argument.
answer: The reason is right and the physics in it is wrong. Parallel wiring gives each appliance the full VOLTAGE, and each then draws the current it needs.
explanation: Every branch of a parallel combination is connected across the same two points, so each appliance sees the full 230 V supply and works at its rated power regardless of what else is switched on. The current is not shared out equally and is certainly not delivered whole to each: each appliance draws I = V ÷ R for its own resistance, and the supply carries the SUM of those currents, which is why a house has a main breaker and why adding appliances increases the total current drawn. In series, by contrast, the supply voltage would divide between appliances, everything would run below its rating, and switching one off would break the circuit for all the others. The learner's conclusion about why parallel is used is correct; the quantity that is shared and the quantity that is common have been swapped.

prompt: A learner predicts that adding a third resistor in parallel to an existing parallel combination must increase the total resistance, "because you have added more resistance to the circuit". Evaluate this prediction.
answer: The prediction is wrong. Adding a parallel branch always DECREASES the total resistance, below even the smallest branch.
explanation: Resistance measures opposition to current for a given potential difference, and a new parallel branch gives the charge an extra route it did not have before. Each branch still carries exactly the current it carried before, because each still has the same voltage across it, and the new branch adds its own current on top — so for the same supply voltage the total current rises, and R = V ÷ I must therefore fall. The arithmetic agrees: 1 ÷ Rp = 1 ÷ R₁ + 1 ÷ R₂ + 1 ÷ R₃, so every term added makes the sum larger and Rp smaller. The learner's intuition comes from series circuits, where a new component sits IN the single path and lengthens it. A useful picture is a doorway: adding another doorway to a hall does not make it harder to leave.

prompt: A learner adds a third identical bulb in series to two already in series with a battery, and predicts the battery will now last three times as long "because the energy is being shared between three bulbs instead of two". Evaluate this prediction.
answer: The prediction is wrong in its reasoning and roughly right in its direction — the battery lasts longer because the current has fallen, not because energy is shared.
explanation: Adding a third bulb raises the total resistance from 2R to 3R, so the current falls from ε ÷ 2R to ε ÷ 3R, two thirds of what it was. A battery's life is governed by the CHARGE it can supply, and at two thirds of the current that charge lasts about one and a half times as long, not three times. The bulbs are also each dimmer than before: each drops one third of the emf instead of one half, and P = I²R falls with the square of the current, so the circuit as a whole converts energy more slowly. That slower rate is the real reason for the longer life. The learner is right that the energy is divided three ways rather than two; what they have missed is that the total being divided has shrunk as well.

prompt: Two identical bulbs X and Y are in parallel across a battery. A third identical bulb Z is connected in parallel with them. A learner predicts X and Y will not change at all, "because each branch still has the full battery voltage across it". Evaluate this prediction.
answer: The prediction is exactly right for an ideal battery and slightly wrong for a real one: X and Y dim a little, because of internal resistance.
explanation: The learner's reasoning is sound as far as it goes. Each branch is connected across the battery's terminals, so each carries V ÷ R, and adding branch Z does not change the voltage across X or Y. If the battery had no internal resistance, X and Y would be unaffected and the only change would be a larger total current. A real battery has internal resistance r, and the terminal voltage is Vterm = ε − Ir. Adding Z lowers the external resistance from R ÷ 2 to R ÷ 3, so the total current rises, the lost volts Ir rise with it, and the terminal voltage falls — so X and Y do dim slightly. The prediction is therefore correct in its physics and incomplete in its model, and the size of the effect is a good test of how good a battery is.

prompt: Two identical bulbs are connected in series to a battery. A learner predicts that unscrewing one of them will make the other brighter, "because all the current will now go through the one that is left". Evaluate this prediction.
answer: The prediction is wrong. Unscrewing one bulb breaks the loop, and the remaining bulb goes out.
explanation: A series circuit is a single path, and current can only flow if that path is complete from one terminal of the battery to the other. Removing a bulb leaves a gap, so the current everywhere in the loop falls to zero and the surviving bulb carries no current at all. The learner is picturing a parallel circuit, where the branches are independent and removing one genuinely does leave the others working — which is why house wiring is parallel, and why one failed lamp does not darken a room. The prediction would be right about a redistribution if the two bulbs had been in parallel and the supply had a fixed voltage. In series, what the second bulb was doing was carrying the same current, not taking a share of it away.

prompt: A learner measures 12 V across a battery's terminals with nothing connected, then 10.5 V while it drives a circuit, and concludes the battery is faulty and losing charge rapidly. Evaluate this conclusion.
answer: The conclusion is wrong. A terminal voltage that drops under load is normal, and the size of the drop measures the internal resistance.
explanation: Every real cell has internal resistance r, from the chemistry and conducting paths inside it. With nothing connected, no current flows, so nothing is lost inside and the voltmeter reads the full emf: ε = 12 V. Once current I flows, the charge must pass through r as well, dropping Ir inside the cell, so what reaches the terminals is Vterm = ε − Ir = 10.5 V. The 1.5 V difference is the lost volts, and if the current were known, r = 1.5 ÷ I could be worked out from it. A genuinely failing battery shows itself differently — its INTERNAL RESISTANCE has risen, so the same load pulls the terminal voltage down much further than it used to. The learner has observed the standard behaviour of a working cell and read it as a fault.

prompt: A learner claims that a bulb of higher resistance always glows more brightly, "because resistance is what converts electrical energy into light". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is true for bulbs in parallel and false for bulbs in series, so it cannot stand as a general rule.
explanation: Brightness follows the power dissipated, and which form of P = VI is useful depends on what the two bulbs share. In PARALLEL, both have the same voltage across them, so P = V² ÷ R and the bulb with the HIGHER resistance dissipates less power and glows more dimly — the opposite of the claim. In SERIES, both carry the same current, so P = I²R and the bulb with the higher resistance does dissipate more and glow more brightly, which is presumably where the learner's rule came from. The underlying error is treating resistance alone as if it decided the outcome, when the quantity held in common by the circuit is what selects which relationship applies. Resistance is where the conversion happens; how much is converted depends on the current and voltage that the circuit delivers to it.

prompt: A learner argues that a short circuit is harmless in itself, "because a wire with almost no resistance uses hardly any energy". Evaluate this argument.
answer: The argument is wrong. Low resistance is exactly what makes a short circuit dangerous, because the current becomes enormous.
explanation: The learner has fixed the current and varied the resistance, when it is the other way round: I = V ÷ R, so as R falls toward zero the current rises without any comparable limit. The power dissipated in the shorting wire is P = I²R, and although R is small, I² grows far faster than R shrinks, so the power is large — a 12 V supply across 0.01 Ω would drive 1 200 A and dissipate over 14 kW in that wire. In practice the current is limited only by the supply's internal resistance, and the wire heats fast enough to melt its insulation or start a fire, while the battery or supply may be damaged by the current it is forced to deliver. Fuses and circuit breakers exist for precisely this case: they are chosen to fail before the wiring does.
